title: ר' טרפון

paragraphs: (a) In the Mishnah: Berakhot 1:3, Berakhot 6:8; Peah 3:6; Kilayim 5:8; Terumot 4:5, Terumot 9:2; Maaserot 3:9; Maaser Sheni 2:4, Maaser Sheni 2:9; Shabbat 2:2; Eruvin 4:4; Pesachim 10:6; Sukkah 3:4; Beitzah 3:5; Taanit 3:9; Yevamot 15:6, Yevamot 15:7; Ketubot 5:2, Ketubot 7:6, Ketubot 9:2, Ketubot 9:3; Nedarim 6:6; Nazir 5:5, Nazir 6:6; Kiddushin 3:13; Bava Kamma 2:5; Bava Metzia 2:7, Bava Metzia 4:3; Makkot 1:10; Avot 2:15; Eduyot 1:10; Zevachim 10:8, Zevachim 11:7; Menachot 12:5; Bekhorot 2:6, Bekhorot 2:7, Bekhorot 2:8, Bekhorot 2:9 and Bekhorot 4:4; Keritot 5:2, Keritot 5:3; Kelim 11:4, Kelim 11:7 and Kelim 25:7; Ohalot 13:3, Ohalot 16:1; Mikvaot 10:5; Yadayim 4:3; Makhshirin 5:4.

(b) He was a priest, as in Kiddushin 71a: “Once I went up after my mother's brother to the platform.” Rashi explains that he was a priest. Tosefta Ketubot 5:1 (Lieberman) records in R. Elazar HaKappar’s name that R. Tarfon betrothed three hundred women to feed them terumah during a drought. Babylonian Pesachim 72b, near the end: R. Tarfon did not come to the study house. Rabban Gamliel found him and asked why. He replied, “I performed service”: he ate terumah, which is called service. An elder met him and said, “People are murmuring against you because you accept terumah from anyone during the rest of the year.” R. Tarfon said, “May I lose my sons! I have a received law from R. Yochanan ben Zakkai, who told me I may accept it. Now I undertake not to accept unless the cask contains a quarter-log of consecrated liquid”: Tosefta, end of Chagigah. Bekhorot 51b: he returned a firstborn's redemption money to its owner. Sifra, Metzora: R. Yehudah said, “It was the Sabbath, and I followed R. Tarfon home. He said, ‘Yehudah my son, give me my sandals.’ I gave them to him. He reached to the window and took a stick from it for me. He said, ‘Yehudah my son, with this I purified three lepers.’ I learned seven laws from him: it was cedar; purification is performed while the Temple stands and when it does not, and outside the Temple, etc.” This too indicates he was a priest. Tractate Middot says his mother was also of priestly descent. Rashi in Kiddushin there likewise seems to explain that he went up after his mother's brother, who was a priest. But Rashi in Ein Yaakov reads: his mother's brother was a Levite, and R. Tarfon was a priest. R. Tarfon followed a Levite to play the flute and other musical instruments, for which everyone is qualified; alternatively, he was a minor and sounded his voice with the young Levites. End of quotation. Sifrei, Behaalotekha; Jerusalem Horayot, chapter 3; Yoma, chapter 1, halakhah 1; Megillah, chapter 1, halakhah 10: “The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow.” R. Akiva says: unblemished men, not blemished ones. R. Tarfon said, “May I lose my sons if I did not see Shimon, my mother's brother, lame in one leg, sounding the trumpets!” He replied, “Yes; perhaps it was at Hakhel, Yom Kippur, or the Jubilee.” He answered, “By the service, you have not invented this! Fortunate are you, Abraham our father, that Akiva emerged from your loins. Tarfon saw and forgot; Akiva expounds on his own and agrees with the law. Whoever parts from you is as though he parts from his life.” There is a similar account in HaOmer, Kiddushin 66b. Megillah there calls R. Tarfon the father of all Israel. Jerusalem Talmud, HaMemunneh, halakhah 7: R. Tarfon said, “I stood in the row among my fellow priests”—Kohelet Rabbah, on “He made everything beautiful in its time,” has “I went up with Shimon, my mother's brother, to the platform”—“and inclined my ear toward the high priest. I heard him swallow the Name within the priests' melodies.” End of quotation. This proves his mother's brother was a priest, contrary to Ein Yaakov's reading.

(c) Yuchasin refers to “Semachot, chapter 6: when R. Shimon ben Yehotzadak died, they asked R. Tarfon.” It is not there, but in chapter 4, halakhah 11. This is puzzling: R. Shimon ben Yehotzadak was R. Yochanan's teacher; how could R. Tarfon live more than two hundred years? The reading before us is: Shimon ben Yehotzadak died at Lod. His brother Yochanan came from Galilee after the grave was closed, seeking to become impure, etc. They asked the sages, who said he should not become impure; let them open the grave for him to see. End of quotation. Thus it was not R. Tarfon who was asked, but the sages. However, I saw in Asheri, Elu Megallechin: Avel Rabbati has an incident in which Yehotzadak died at Lod, his brother Yochanan came from Galilee after the grave was closed, and they asked R. Tarfon. Even this reading, which says R. Tarfon was asked, does not mention R. Shimon ben Yehotzadak, only that Yehotzadak died, so there is no basis for the difficulty. Furthermore, even Semachot's reading says Shimon ben Yehotzadak, whereas R. Yochanan's teacher is called R. Shimon ben Yehotzadak. Likewise, Bekhorot, chapter 1, says Rabbi brought him a firstborn donkey. How could R. Tarfon live until Rabbi's days? Rabbi was born on the day R. Akiva died, and R. Tarfon preceded R. Akiva and was like his teacher: he would have lived many years. Perhaps it was Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, who was also called Rabbi. See there: he was called Berabbi, rather than Rabbi. See Keitzad Mevarkhin, where R. Tarfon told Rabban Gamliel, “You taught us, our teacher.” But the attempted answer that the “Rabbi” who brought the firstborn donkey was Rabban Gamliel, rather than R. Yehudah HaNasi, is incorrect. Our text in Bekhorot, chapter 1, 11a, beginning, says R. Yehudah Nesia had a firstborn donkey and brought it to R. Tarfon. So too Asheri and Yalkut, Tissa, section 402. One cannot say he had a Gemara reading “Rabbi had a firstborn donkey,” for in the aforementioned letter tet he himself cited “R. Yehudah Nesia had a firstborn donkey and brought it to R. Tarfon.” The difficulty is actually greater: how could R. Tarfon live until R. Yehudah Nesia, our holy Rabbi's grandson?

(d) Gittin 67a and Avot DeRabbi Natan: he was called a heap of nuts. Bereshit Rabbah, section 91: when someone said something sound, he said, “Knob and blossom”; otherwise he said, “My son shall not go down with you.” In the Mishnah in Ad Kamma, Bekhorot 28b, near the end, R. Tarfon fed a cow to dogs, but the sages at Yavneh permitted it. R. Tarfon said, “Your donkey is gone, Tarfon!” R. Akiva told him, “You are an expert for the court and exempt from payment”: Sanhedrin 33. Tractate Kallah says R. Tarfon was exceedingly wealthy but did not give charity. R. Akiva met him and said, “Would you like me to buy you a town or two?” He immediately gave him four thousand gold dinars. R. Akiva took them and distributed them to the poor. Later R. Tarfon met him and asked where the towns he had bought were. He took him by the hand, led him to the study house, brought a Book of Psalms, and set it before him. They read until reaching “He dispersed, he gave to the needy, etc.” He said, “This is the town I bought you.” R. Tarfon rose, kissed his head, and said, “My teacher and my guide: my teacher in wisdom and my guide in proper conduct.” See Rabbah, end of Behar. Nedarim 62a and Jerusalem Sheviit, chapter 4: R. Tarfon ate figs. A man found him, put him in a sack, and wished to throw him into the river. He said, “Woe to Tarfon, whom this man is killing!” He released him. R. Tarfon was distressed all his life for using the crown of Torah. Gilgulei Neshamot (ג״נ), Tet §1, writes that R. Tarfon is Jeremiah. His being put in a sack to be thrown into the river alludes to Jeremiah, who prophesied concerning the two baskets of figs; Jeremiah too was thrown into a pit and saved, and was a priest. Jerusalem Demai, chapter 1: he sat to eat, and his bread fell from his mouth because he had borrowed an axe and used it over pure things. Kiddushin 31b and Jerusalem Kiddushin, chapter 1, halakhah 7: how he honored his mother. Kiddushin 81b: he would not seclude himself with his daughter-in-law. A student mocked him and stumbled with his own mother-in-law, for all the sages' words are true. End of Avot DeRabbi Natan: while R. Tarfon studied with his students, a bride passed. He ordered her brought to his house and told his mother and wife, “Wash her, anoint her, adorn her, and dance before her until she goes to her husband's house.” Menachot 68b and Sifrei, Pinchas, passage “On the day of the first fruits,” differ somewhat in wording. So too Yuchasin, in the sequence of generations under the second group after the destruction. Sifrei reads: R. Tarfon said, “Meal offerings brought before the two loaves should be invalid.” R. Yehudah bar Nachman—Menachot has bar Nechemyah—said, “No; if you said, etc.” R. Akiva looked at him, and his face brightened. He said, “Your face brightened because you answered the elder! I wonder whether you will live long.” R. Elazar son of R. Yehudah—the Gemara has R. Yehudah bar Ilai—said: it occurred at Passover; the Gemara has shortly before Passover. At Shavuot I asked, “Where is R. Yehudah bar Nachman”—Nechemyah? They told me, “He has gone.” End of quotation. Rashi, Yevamot, chapter 1, says he was of Beit Shammai. Evidence for Rashi: Berakhot, chapter 1, R. Tarfon says he reclined to recite like Beit Shammai. He regularly swore, “May I lose my sons”: Zevachim 13a; Mishnah Ohalot, chapter 16; Shabbat, chapter 1, 17a, beginning, and there, 116a; also mentioned above. Bava Metzia, chapter 5: Rabbi asked whether R. Tarfon, who used to say “May I lose my sons,” had left a son. They said he left only a daughter and her son. Rabbi taught the grandson Torah and gave him his daughter; some say he did not marry her. But Shevuat HaDayyanim, Shevuot 39b, teaches “R. Shimon son of R. Tarfon says,” and Kol HaNishbain, Shevuot 47b, has four laws. Perhaps this was during his father's lifetime. It mentions only the unqualified “ben Tarfon,” rather than “R. Tarfon” [the source's qualification]. Jerusalem Yevamot, chapter 4, halakhah 11; Semachot, chapter 7: when R. Tarfon's wife died, he told her sister, “Go support your sister's children.” See a similar account above under R. Yosi the priest.

(e) He was R. Yosi HaGelili’s teacher and R. Akiva’s. For Akiva, see Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 45a, although the Passover Haggadah mentions R. Akiva before R. Tarfon. But HaIshah in Yevamot and HaKotev, Ketubot 84b, raise doubt in the Gemara whether he was R. Akiva's teacher or colleague. Asheri rules there like R. Akiva, since he was R. Tarfon's colleague, and the law follows R. Akiva against his colleague. See R. Akiva on the legal decision, although Sifrei has R. Akiva saying, “My teacher, permit me to say one thing.” Shenot Chayyim, VeZot HaBerakhah, 218b, beginning, writes: “Keneset HaGedolah hesitates whether R. Tarfon was R. Akiva's teacher or colleague. I found it explicit in Torat Kohanim, Vayikra: R. Tarfon said, ‘Akiva, etc.’ He replied, ‘Permit me to say what you taught me.’ Thus he was R. Tarfon's student, both because he called him Akiva and because he said ‘Permit me.’” Yadayim, chapter 4, has R. Eliezer ben Yaakov—I think it should read R. Elazar ben Azaryah—calling R. Tarfon “my brother.” R. Yehudah said, “Once we were sitting before R. Tarfon”: Kiddushin 14a; Yevamot 101b. He spoke in R. Tarfon's name: end of Chalon, Eruvin 82a; Sukkah 32a; Niddah 38a; see above. R. Yehudah also read the Megillah before R. Tarfon when he was a minor.

(f) Abba Shaul of Ramsha, his teacher. R. Oshaya son of R. Yehudah the perfumer testified in his name. R. Elazar HaModai and R. Yishmael sat; see there. Yuchasin, under R. Meir, writes that R. Meir apparently was his student, since he reached his shoulder, as in Niddah 24b; all mentioned there were teacher and student. But I saw in Tosafot, Yevamot 86a, that R. Elazar ben Azaryah long preceded R. Meir; all the more R. Tarfon long preceded R. Meir. How, then, could R. Meir be his student? See Abba Shaul. Rava said concerning him, “May the Master forgive him”: Sukkah 32b. R. Shimon Shezuri questioned him.
